description: Four factors that shape your price and the four pricing strategies every start-up needs to know.
content_html:
Why Pricing Is One of the Most Important Decisions a Start-Up Makes

Getting the price right matters enormously for a new business. Set it too high and customers will go elsewhere. Set it too low and the business will not cover its costs, let alone make a profit. Price is also a signal — customers make judgements about quality based on what something costs. A handmade ceramic vase priced at an extremely low level may feel untrustworthy, while the same vase priced confidently communicates craft and care.

Before choosing a pricing strategy, an entrepreneur should think carefully about four key factors that shape the decision.

Four Factors That Influence Pricing

The more money a target customer earns, the more they are likely to be willing to spend on a product. A business selling to higher-income customers can justify a premium price and use that price to signal quality and exclusivity. A business selling to lower-income customers needs to keep the price accessible — if the price feels out of reach, customers will walk away regardless of how good the product is.

When customers can easily compare prices — as they can on almost any digital channel — charging significantly more than competitors is risky unless the business can clearly justify the difference. A new coffee shop opening near several established competitors must think about what local customers currently pay, because pricing dramatically higher will deter potential customers who have other options.

A business must always know what it costs to make or source each unit. If the price does not cover those costs, every sale generates a loss. This does not mean the price is purely determined by cost — but cost sets a floor below which the business cannot sustainably trade. If production costs rise (for instance, the price of raw materials increases), the business faces a difficult choice: absorb the cost, reduce profit margins, or pass it on to customers through a price rise.

The appropriate price changes as the product moves through its lifecycle. At introduction, a brand-new product with no competition may be able to sustain a high price because early adopters will pay a premium. As the product matures and more competitors enter, the business may need to review its price to stay competitive. At decline, a price reduction may be used as an extension strategy to attract price-sensitive customers who were previously put off.

Key Fact

Four factors influence a business’s pricing decision: income levels of target customers (determines what they can afford), competitor prices (sets a reference point customers will use), cost of production (the floor below which the business makes a loss) and stage of the product lifecycle (shapes how much premium or discount the market will accept).

The Four Pricing Strategies

A pricing strategy is the deliberate approach a business takes to pricing — not just picking a number, but choosing a method that fits the product, the customer and the competition. There are four strategies that a start-up needs to know.

Competitive pricing means pricing in line with rivals. This is common in markets where products are broadly similar and customers will compare prices before buying — think of local takeaway menus or supermarket own-brand products. The advantage is that the business does not risk losing customers purely on price. The risk is that margins can be thin, especially if a price war develops where all competitors keep cutting.

Psychological pricing exploits the way customers perceive numbers. A product priced just below a round number feels significantly cheaper, even though the actual difference is small. A craft gin bottle presented at a price just below a round-number threshold feels like a bargain compared with the same bottle at the round number, even though the difference is minor. This strategy suits consumer goods where the buying decision is partly emotional.

Price skimming involves setting a high price at launch and reducing it over time. It works when the product is genuinely new, in demand, and has no close competition. Early adopters — customers who want to be first — are willing to pay a premium for exclusivity. As the novelty fades and competitors appear, the price is lowered to reach a broader market. This strategy suits innovative or distinctive products rather than everyday commodities.

Penetration pricing does the opposite: the launch price is deliberately low to attract customers away from established competitors and build market share fast. The business accepts lower — or even negative — margins initially, betting that once customers are loyal they will stay even if the price rises. This suits new entrants to a competitive market where the established players have higher prices.

Key Fact

The four pricing strategies are: competitive (match rivals to avoid losing on price), psychological (price just below a round number to feel like a bargain), skimming (high at launch to maximise early revenue, then reduce) and penetration (low at launch to win market share, then raise). No single strategy is always best — the right choice depends on the product, the market and the competition.

Choosing the Right Strategy

The four influencing factors and the four strategies work together. Consider Millbrook Candle Co., a new small candle start-up in Cardiff. Its customers are mid-income gift buyers. Its costs are modest. There are several established candle brands in the same price bracket. A skimming strategy would struggle here because the product is not genuinely new or scarce. A penetration strategy might win customers initially but thin margins on a low-volume product could cause cash flow problems. Competitive pricing — matching the established brands while using psychological pricing on individual lines — would be a sensible starting point, giving the business a foothold without a price war.

Remember: the spec states that worked pricing examples should be about the type of strategy chosen and why, not about calculating a specific price figure. You will not be asked to work out a price in a formula — you will be asked to recommend and justify a strategy based on the context given.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Explain or 6-mark Analyse question on pricing, always connect your chosen strategy to the specific start-up in the question — name its product, its customer type, or its competitive situation. A generic answer describing what penetration pricing is without linking it to why it suits this business will stall in the Developing tier. For 6-mark Justify questions, the command word “justify” requires good reasons for your recommendation, not just a description. Build a reason chain using “because” and “this means that” to connect strategy to business outcome. This lesson also feeds into the extended-response evaluation question on the marketing mix, which always appears in the written exam — pricing strategy is one of the four Ps and must work alongside product, place and promotion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pricing decisions are shaped by four factors: income levels of target customers, competitor prices, cost of production and the stage of the product lifecycle.
  • The four pricing strategies are competitive (match rivals), psychological (price just below a round number), skimming (high launch price then reduce) and penetration (low launch price to build share). The right choice depends on the product, market and competitive context.
  • In exam questions, justify your recommended strategy with reason chains linked to the scenario — do not just define the strategy. The extended-response evaluation question on the marketing mix rewards answers that show how pricing connects to the other three Ps.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes price skimming?
A) Setting a price in line with competitors to avoid losing customers on price
B) Launching at a low price to win market share quickly, then raising it later
C) Launching at a high price to earn maximum revenue from early adopters, then reducing it
D) Pricing just below a round number to make the product feel cheaper
practice_questions.marks: C) Launching at a high price to earn maximum revenue from early adopters, then reducing it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two factors that might influence the price a new business charges for its product.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any two of the following (1 mark for one correct answer on a 1-mark Identify question — if the instruction calls for two, treat this as a 2-mark response and award 1 mark each):
• Income levels of target customers
• Competitor prices
• Cost of production
• Stage of the product lifecycle
[1 mark for one correctly identified factor]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between penetration pricing and price skimming.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each accurately described strategy, up to 2 marks:
• Penetration pricing sets a low price at launch to win customers quickly, with the intention of raising the price later [1 mark]
• Price skimming sets a high price at launch to maximise revenue from early adopters, then reduces it as competition enters [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Hartwell Audio is a small start-up in Bristol that has developed a wireless speaker with genuinely new sound technology. There are no direct competitors at launch. Its target customers are music enthusiasts aged 25-45 with mid-to-high incomes.

Explain one pricing strategy that would be appropriate for Hartwell Audio at the launch stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Full marks for one fully developed point:
• Price skimming would be appropriate for Hartwell Audio (1 mark) because the product has genuinely new technology with no direct competition at launch (1 mark), which means early adopters who want to be first will pay a premium price (1 mark), allowing Hartwell Audio to earn high revenue in the early stage before competitors enter and force a price reduction (1 mark).
[Accept penetration pricing as a valid alternative with a developed and logical reason chain — e.g. that winning early market share quickly builds brand recognition before competitors arrive; award up to 4 marks for a well-developed and logically consistent chain.]

practice_questions.text:
Copper & Croft is a small sustainable homeware brand based in Edinburgh, run by founder Jess. She sells hand-stitched linen napkins. Her production costs are low, her target customers are mid-income households, and she is entering a market where several established brands already trade at similar quality levels.

Analyse which pricing strategy would be most appropriate for Copper & Croft.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Student identifies a specific strategy and develops two or more analytical points connecting all relevant contextual factors (mid-income customers, existing competition, low production cost, homeware market). The response shows awareness of trade-offs and reaches a supported conclusion about which strategy fits best and why the others would be less appropriate.

Secure (3-4 marks): One strategy is recommended with developed reasoning and at least one contextual link. Some reference to the competitive environment or customer income level.

Developing (2 marks): A strategy is named with a brief and mostly correct explanation, but the link to the specific business context is limited or absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A pricing strategy is named with a very brief or partially incorrect description.

practice_questions.text:
Vanta Coffee Co. is a new independent coffee brand launched in Manchester by founder Rahul. He is targeting busy office workers who currently buy coffee from large chain cafes. His coffee is of comparable quality to the established chains but his costs are lower.

Rahul is deciding between two pricing strategies:
Option A: Penetration pricing — launch at a noticeably lower price than the chains to attract customers quickly.
Option B: Competitive pricing — match the chains' prices and compete on quality and service.

Justify which pricing strategy you would recommend to Rahul.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified using specific contextual details (office workers, comparable quality, lower costs, large-chain competition). The student develops the reasons for the chosen strategy, addresses a key drawback and explains why it does not override the recommendation in this context. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with clear reasoning and some use of context. At least one drawback is acknowledged.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning but context is used only superficially. Analysis is limited.

Emerging (1 mark): A strategy is named with little or no reasoned justification.

knowledge_checks.q: Which pricing strategy involves launching at a low price to gain market share and then raising it?
Which factor influences pricing by setting the minimum price a business can sustain?
Setting a price at a similar level to competitors so that price is not the main reason customers choose or reject the product is called _____ pricing.
Pricing a product at £9.99 instead of £10.00 to make it feel cheaper is an example of _____ pricing.
Match each pricing strategy to the situation where it is most appropriate:
right: A new innovative product with no direct competition and enthusiastic early adopters
A new entrant to a competitive market wanting to win customers quickly
A consumer product sold in a retail environment where buyers make emotional decisions

flashcard_questions.a: Setting a price at a similar level to rivals so price is not the deciding factor for customers.
Pricing just below a round number so the product feels cheaper to customers.
Launching at a high price to earn maximum revenue from early adopters, then reducing it.
Launching at a low price to win customers quickly, then raising the price once they are loyal.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four factors that influence a business's pricing decision.
flashcard_questions.a: Customer income levels, competitor prices, cost of production, stage of the product lifecycle.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a price always cover the cost of production?
flashcard_questions.a: If the price is below cost, every sale generates a loss and the business cannot survive.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a new product with no competition use price skimming?
flashcard_questions.a: Early adopters will pay a premium for exclusivity before competitors enter the market.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the risk of using penetration pricing at launch?
flashcard_questions.a: Low margins may cause cash flow problems before the price can be raised.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the product lifecycle stage affect pricing?
flashcard_questions.a: A new product can sustain higher prices; a declining product may need a price cut to attract buyers.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does competitive pricing require tight cost control?
flashcard_questions.a: Matching rivals' prices leaves little room to raise margins, so profit depends on keeping costs low.

flashcard_questions.q: In an exam pricing question, what should you always do alongside naming a strategy?
flashcard_questions.a: Link the strategy to the specific business context using a reason chain.

glossary_terms.definition: The approach a business takes to setting the price of its product, based on its objectives, the competitive environment and the target market.
Setting a price at a similar level to competitors, so that price is not the main reason customers choose or reject the product.
Using a price that ends in .99 or .95 to make a product feel cheaper than a round number, even though the difference is tiny.
Launching a new product at a high price to earn maximum revenue from early adopters, then gradually lowering the price as competition increases.
Launching a new product at a low price to win customers quickly and build a large market share, with the intention of raising the price later.
